messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 35
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: Oceania
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Accountant
- Trauma Type: Mugging or robbery
- Pcl5: 71

The mugging happened on a Tuesday evening in early autumn, just after she left the office. She is an accountant for a mid-sized firm, and that night she had stayed late to reconcile a client’s quarterly report. The numbers had been stubborn, and she remembers feeling satisfied as she finally locked her office door. The walk to the train station was a route she had taken hundreds of times—past the coffee shop, under the old railway bridge, through the narrow alley that cut between two parking garages. She never thought twice about it.

He came from behind. She didn’t see his face, only felt the shove that sent her shoulder into the brick wall, then the hard tug on her bag strap. She tried to hold on—her laptop, her notes, her wallet—but the strap snapped and he was gone, boots slapping the wet pavement. She stood there for a long moment, breathing in the smell of damp stone and diesel, her hands shaking. A passerby asked if she was okay, and she said yes, because what else was there to say? She walked the rest of the way to the station with her arms crossed over her chest, her empty hands cold.

That was seven months ago. She still works at the same firm, still balances spreadsheets and files tax returns, but something inside her has shifted, like a piece of furniture she can’t push back into place. She no longer stays late. At four thirty, her stomach tightens and she starts packing her bag, even if the numbers aren’t finished. She tells herself it’s just efficiency, but her supervisor has noticed. Three times she has left a meeting early, claiming a headache, because the conference room has only one door and she couldn’t stop thinking about someone coming through it.

Her desk is in a cubicle near the elevator bank. Every time the elevator chimes, her shoulders jump. She has learned to keep her back to the wall in the break room, even if it means standing instead of sitting with her coffee. The smallest noises—a dropped pen, a slammed drawer—make her heart punch against her ribs. She checks the lock on her office door four or five times before she can settle into work, and she has started carrying a small can of pepper spray in her purse, even though she never leaves the building except to go home.

Home is no longer the safe place it used to be. She and her husband, a high school teacher, used to take evening walks around their neighborhood. Now she refuses. If he suggests a walk, she says she’s tired. If he pushes, her voice goes sharp and she walks away. She knows he is trying to help, but the thought of being outside in the dark, of hearing footsteps behind them, makes her feel like she is drowning. At night she wakes up gasping, her hands clutching the sheets, her body drenched in sweat. In the dream, the strap never breaks. He pulls her down, and she cannot get up.

She has stopped meeting friends for dinner. The noise of a restaurant—the clatter of plates, the loud laughter—feels too big, too unpredictable. She finds herself scanning faces instead of listening to conversations. Last month, at her sister’s birthday party, she spent half the night standing in the kitchen, watching the back door. When her husband asked what was wrong, she said nothing. But she knows it’s not nothing.

At work, her concentration has frayed. Numbers that once lined up neatly now blur. She rechecks each row three times, then still doubts herself. She has missed two deadlines, something that never happened before. She feels distant from her colleagues, as though a glass wall has slid down between her and the chatter around the coffee machine. She hears them talk about weekend plans, and she can’t remember when she last had one.

She doesn’t think about the mugging during the day—not deliberately. But the memory surfaces in flashes: the scrape of the brick on her shoulder, the grunt of the man’s breath, the taste of fear, metallic and sharp. She pushes it away. She tells herself she is fine, that it was just a bag, that she should be grateful she wasn’t hurt worse. But the guilt sits in her chest like a stone. She should have fought harder. She should have screamed. She should have been smarter, stayed in the office longer, taken a different route.

She has stopped taking the train. She drives to work now, even though parking costs half her lunch budget. The drive takes longer, but she controls the doors, the windows, the radio. She hasn’t been back to that alley. She takes the long way around, even if it means adding ten minutes to her commute. She doesn’t tell anyone why.

Her husband asked her last week if she wanted to talk to someone. She said no. But she is here, in my office, because she finally couldn’t stand the weight of it anymore—the constant checking, the waking up afraid, the feeling that the world has become a place where anything can happen, at any moment, when she least expects it.
